prose.def: The act of gathering or being brought together into one assembly or group.
prose.article: ἐπισυναγωγή refers to the act of bringing or coming together into one assembly. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders both as "together" — once for believers meeting (Hebrews 10:25) and once for being gathered to Christ (2 Thessalonians 2:1). The word was once thought unknown outside the Bible, but Deissmann found it on a pre-100 BC inscription from the island of Syme, where it meant the "collection" of a sum of money to cover expenses.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and very thin attestation, confidence in the full range of this word is low.

receipts.how: 'Not forsaking the assembling (ἐπισυναγωγήν) of yourselves together' — the noun clearly denotes the concrete meeting-event of believers, supporting the 'assembly' sense the current definition underweights.
'Our gathering together (ἐπισυναγωγῆς) unto him' — here the noun refers to an eschatological gathering to Christ, showing the word covers both ecclesial assembly and apocalyptic ingathering.

Used with the genitive 'unto him (ἐπ᾽ αὐτόν)', demonstrating the word functions as a standalone noun denoting the act-and-result of being assembled, not merely an adverbial modifier — the current definition's process-only framing is partially misleading.

audit.author_note: Paul (2 Thessalonians) uses the word for an eschatological, Christ-directed gathering, while the author of Hebrews applies it to the regular communal assembly of believers — readers of each should be aware the referent differs significantly.

prose.def: To come rushing together toward one spot, as a crowd quickly gathering at a particular place or occasion.
prose.article: This verb describes people swarming or rushing together toward a single place, built from prefixes meaning "upon" and "together" attached to a verb for running. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Mark 9:25, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "come running" and the Berean Standard Bible agrees fully. Notably, Moulton-Milligan could find no actual papyrus citation of this exact word, though the closely related ἐπιτρέχω shows up as the title of a village inspector or overseer in everyday documents.

prose.def: A hostile gathering or crowd that rises up against someone, sometimes the pressure of such opposition.
prose.article: ἐπισύστασις pictures people banding together against someone—a riotous throng or hostile combination. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament and is absent from the critical SBLGNT text, where editors prefer the similar word ἐπίστασις instead. The Majority Standard Bible renders it once as 'accusers' (Acts 24:12) and once as 'trials' (2 Corinthians 11:28), and an inscription from the first century B.C. uses it of 'risings up' by hostile barbarians, reinforcing the idea of organized opposition.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin—only two disputed New Testament occurrences, the critical text omits the word entirely, and the two measured renderings ('accusers' and 'trials') pull in noticeably different directions.

prose.def: Describing something risky or precarious, likely to cause a fall or lead to harm.
prose.article: This adjective describes a situation that is unsafe or likely to lead to a fall — in the New Testament it appears just once, in Acts 27:9, where sailing had become 'dangerous' as the season turned. It comes from a word meaning to trip or cause to fall, so the literal idea of being 'prone to fall' (noted by Plato and Abbott-Smith) shades into the figurative sense of being 'insecure' or precarious. A nice everyday parallel comes from a papyrus letter (P Oxy 76, A.D. 179), where the related adverb describes a person who 'has fallen ill and is in a precarious condition.'
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is used only by Luke, so its New Testament range is very thin.
